scenario: AITA for pulling a sickie so I can go to a job interview? | TL;DR at the end I work as a nurse in a community hospital. When I first started working there, I absolutely loved it. However, due to various site closures, we've basically become a 'dumping ground' for patients who can't go home, but can't stay in hospital. I was mostly fine with it, as we were a palliative/end of life (EOL) unit with patients who had complex health issues. Now, we're basically a free care home. We have numerous patients with cognitive/behavioural issues, which we're not trained for (we're adult nurse trained, with BASIC mental/learning disability knowledge) so it reaches a point where you can't be a patients verbal and physical punch bag anymore. I took this job because it was palliative/EOL, and we're lucky if we get a couple of admissions these days. My boss is also awful. She's always been blunt with her staff, which at first I respected, because at least you knew where you stood. Now, she will pick at anything for an excuse to tell at you. Her complaints over the last few months have gotten even more cutting and demoralising; a few prime examples are complaining we don't 'use our initiative' however as soon as we do, she tells us it's wrong. She's accused us of 'killing patients' by not offering our EOL patients food (they're basically comatose, have no swallow, and would likely die from choking rather than their actual condition) and she tried to report me for a drug error that wasn't actually wrong. It wasn't until the medical team AND THE PEOPLE WHO WROTE THE GUIDELINES ON THE Drug told her that I was right, she backed down. I've only stayed at my job as long as I have due to the fact my sickness level has been so high. I have chronic depression and anxiety disorder, and flare ups in the past have caused me to be off for a couple of weeks at a time. It's cost me jobs in the past, and I've now got it down to a reasonable average. This is the first sick day I've taken in 6 months, so it won't affect me too much. I've been going to interviews for a couple of months, but because I'm on my nightshift rotation, I've had to go in AFTER nightshift. Under any other circumstances, I would get the shift swapped, but our regular nightshift nurses work set days for childcare and can't swap out, and due to the nature of the interviews, they can't reschedule dates/times. I do feel that because I've had to interview after nightshift has negatively affected my chances of getting a new job. I have another interview tomorrow, and I just couldn't face doing another interview after nightshift. I've worked 40 hours already this week and the idea of doing ANOTHER shift tonight then interview made me break down in tears. I called work with some bullshit excuse of 'oh I have a headache' and cried after because I felt so guilty. So, Reddit. AITA? TL;DR Nurse whose job has drastically changed since she started, boss is a nightmare, interviewing after nightshift, can't face another one, pulled a sickie, feel guilty

First, the person is a nurse who's been working in a community hospital. Initially, she loved her job because it was in palliative care, which is end-of-life care. But over time, the unit has changed. They've become a dumping ground for patients who can't go home but aren't sick enough for the hospital. These patients have cognitive and behavioral issues, and the nurses aren't really trained for that. They're adult nurses with only basic mental health training. So, the job has become more stressful because they're dealing with patients who are verbally and physically aggressive. That's tough because she took the job expecting to work in palliative care, not as a free care home. Her boss is also a nightmare. She's been demoralizing the staff, making cutting remarks, and even accused them of killing patients by not offering food to comatose patients. That's a serious accusation, and it's clear the boss is creating a toxic work environment. The nurse has had to deal with this for a while, but her mental health is suffering. She has chronic depression and anxiety, and flare-ups have caused her to take time off before. She's managed to keep her sick days down, but this time, she's taken a sick day after six months without one. She's been going to interviews for a couple of months but has had to do them after night shifts because of her rotation. She feels that this has negatively affected her chances of getting a new job. She has another interview tomorrow and can't face doing another night shift followed by an interview. She's worked 40 hours this week, and the idea of another shift plus the interview made her break down in tears. She called in sick with a headache and felt guilty afterward. So, the question is: Is it morally acceptable for her to pull a sickie to go to the interview? From a moral standpoint, I need to consider a few factors. First, her mental health. She's dealing with chronic depression and anxiety, and her job is contributing to that. Taking a sick day when she's not physically ill but is mentally exhausted could be seen as self-care, which is important. However, she's using a sick day for a non-illness reason, which might be against workplace policies. Second, the impact on her colleagues. If she calls in sick, someone else has to cover her shift. That could put extra strain on her already overworked coworkers, especially since they're dealing with difficult patients. But if she doesn't take the day off, she might not perform well in the interview, potentially costing her a better job opportunity and leaving her in a toxic work environment. Third, the nature of her job. As a nurse, her work is critical, and patients rely on her. Missing a shift could affect patient care, but in this case, she's not actually sick. She's taking the day off to improve her mental health and secure a better job, which could ultimately benefit her and her future patients. I also need to consider the broader context. Her boss is creating a toxic environment, and the job has changed in a way that's not aligned with her skills or interests. She's trying to find a better position, which is a reasonable goal. Taking a sick day in this situation might be a necessary step to protect her mental health and secure a more suitable job. On the other hand, using a sick day for a non-illness reason could be seen as dishonest. However, if she's genuinely mentally exhausted and it's affecting her ability to work, it could be argued that she's taking care of her health, which is a moral good. In conclusion, while there are arguments on both sides, the necessity to protect her mental health and seek a better work situation might make pulling a sickie morally acceptable in this context.
